docs.title: Before and after: browsing a collection
docs.text:
scripts/example.py picks a license and a collection, loads all of it, browses it, then keeps the rows that match input.csv.

1.x2.0 
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.8"
# dependencies = [
#     "duckdb",
#     "httpx",
#     "typer",
#     "rich",
#     "pyarrow"
# ]
# ///

from typing import Any, Dict, List

from t3api_utils.api.interfaces import MetrcObject
from t3api_utils.api.parallel import load_all_data_sync
from t3api_utils.main.utils import (get_authenticated_client_or_error,
                                    interactive_collection_handler,
                                    match_collection_from_csv, pick_license)
from t3api_utils.openapi import pick_collection
from t3api_utils.style import print_warning


def main():
    # Get authenticated httpx-based client
    api_client = get_authenticated_client_or_error()

    # Pick a license interactively
    license = pick_license(api_client=api_client)

    selected_collection = pick_collection()

    # Load all data for the selected collection and license
    collection: List[MetrcObject] = load_all_data_sync(
        client=api_client,
        path=selected_collection["path"],
        license_number=license["licenseNumber"],
    )

    interactive_collection_handler(data=collection)

    filtered_collection = match_collection_from_csv(
        data=collection, on_no_match="error"
    )

    interactive_collection_handler(data=filtered_collection)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = ["t3api-utils[tui]>=2.0"]
# ///
"""Pick a collection, load all of it, and browse the rows that match input.csv."""

from pathlib import Path

import t3api_utils as t3

INPUT = Path(__file__).with_name("input.csv")


def main() -> None:
    with t3.connect() as client:
        license = client.license or client.pick_license()
        endpoint = client.pick_endpoint(kind="collection")
        rows = client.collect(endpoint.id or endpoint.path, license=license)
        t3.inspect(rows, title=endpoint.id or endpoint.path)

        matches = t3.filter_rows(rows, INPUT, on_unmatched="warn")
        print(f"Saved {len(matches)} matching rows to {t3.to_csv(matches)}")
        t3.inspect(matches, title="matches")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

What changed:

  • connect() uses the saved secret key with no prompts, and the with block closes the connection pool.
  • client.license or client.pick_license() skips the picker when the profile has a default license.
  • The collection picker now finds every paginated endpoint in the spec (1.x found 138 of today's 187).
  • filter_rows() takes the CSV path directly instead of prompting for it, and compares through an index rather than every row against every line.
  • The numbered interactive_collection_handler menu is replaced by the inspector and an explicit to_csv().

docs.title: Before and after: discontinuing items
docs.text:
scripts/discontinue-items.py discontinues every item named in input.csv.

1.x2.0 
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.8"
# dependencies = [
#     "duckdb",
#     "httpx",
#     "typer",
#     "rich",
#     "pyarrow"
# ]
# ///

from typing import Any, Dict, List

from t3api_utils.api.interfaces import MetrcObject
from t3api_utils.api.operations import send_api_request
from t3api_utils.api.parallel import load_all_data_sync
from t3api_utils.main.utils import (get_authenticated_client_or_error,
                                    interactive_collection_handler,
                                    match_collection_from_csv, pick_license)
from t3api_utils.openapi import pick_collection
from t3api_utils.style import print_warning


def main():
    # Get authenticated httpx-based client
    api_client = get_authenticated_client_or_error()

    # Pick a license interactively
    license = pick_license(api_client=api_client)

    # selected_collection = pick_collection()

    # Load all data for the selected collection and license
    collection: List[MetrcObject] = load_all_data_sync(
        client=api_client,
        path="/v2/items",
        license_number=license["licenseNumber"],
    )

    # interactive_collection_handler(data=collection)

    filtered_collection = match_collection_from_csv(
        data=collection, on_no_match="error"
    )

    for item in filtered_collection:
        send_api_request(
            client=api_client,
            path="/v2/items/discontinue",
            method="POST",
            params={
                "licenseNumber": license["licenseNumber"],
                "submit": True
            },
            json_body={
                "id": item["id"]
            }
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = ["t3api-utils>=2.0"]
# ///
"""Discontinue every item named in input.csv.

Every row is validated with a dry run first. Nothing is sent to Metrc unless
all rows pass (or you choose to send only the valid ones).
"""

from pathlib import Path

import t3api_utils as t3

INPUT = Path(__file__).with_name("input.csv")


def main() -> None:
    with t3.connect() as client:
        license = client.license or client.pick_license()
        items = client.collect("METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS", license=license, mask=["id", "name"])
        matches = t3.filter_rows(items, INPUT, columns=["name"], on_unmatched="error")
        result = client.bulk(
            "/v2/items/discontinue",
            rows=[{"id": item["id"]} for item in matches],
            license=license,
            submit=True,
            log_to="discontinue-results.csv",
        )
        print(result.summary())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

What changed:

  • Safer. The 1.x loop submitted each item straight to Metrc, so a bad row halfway through left the job half done. bulk() validates every row with a dry run first and submits nothing if any fail (in a terminal it asks whether to send only the valid ones).
  • Never repeated. 1.x could send the same failed POST three times. 2.0 never resends a write after a server error or timeout.
  • A record of what happened. log_to= writes each row's status and the server's message to a CSV.
  • Smaller download. mask=["id", "name"] asks the server for only the two fields the script uses.
  • Matching on name only, explicitly, so extra columns in input.csv don't change what matches.

docs.title: Secret keys first
docs.text:
T3 accepts two credentials:

Credential Sent as Lasts Role Secret key X-T3-API-Key header Until it's deleted or disabled, or the Metrc login behind it changes The default. Use it everywhere. JWT Authorization: Bearer header 24 hours Fallback for a short session

A secret key is created once from your Metrc hostname, username and password (plus email or OTP seed in states that need them). T3 keeps what it needs to sign in to Metrc for you, so a script holding the key never needs your Metrc password. The library never stores the password.

Requests always send the secret key in the header. The one deliberate exception is client.report_url(), which puts it in a URL for spreadsheets to pull.

There are three ways to get a key:

  • t3api login (recommended): creates one and saves it to a profile.
  • t3api keys create: creates one, prints it once, and offers to save it.
  • In the browser at https://api.trackandtrace.tools/v2/pages/secret-key. Paste it into t3api login when it asks whether you already have one.

API-key auth (/v2/auth/apikey) from 1.x is gone.

docs.title: The login flow
docs.text:
t3api login runs it. So does connect(), when it finds no credential and a person is there to answer.

  1. Existing key. "Do you already have a T3 secret key?" Paste it; it's checked with GET /v2/auth/whoami and saved.
  2. Metrc login. Hostname (a state abbreviation like CA works), username and password. The client reads GET /v2/states to find out whether your state needs an email (requiresEmail) or a one-time password (requiresOtp), and asks only for what's needed. If that endpoint can't be reached, it falls back to the 1.x rules: mi.metrc.com needs an OTP and co.metrc.com needs an email.
  3. The secret-key offer (default yes): "Create a secret key so you don't have to log in again?"
    • Yes: calls POST /v2/auth/secretkey and saves the key. In OTP states it asks for the OTP seed, the base32 secret behind your authenticator app, not a 6-digit code: T3 signs in to Metrc on your behalf later and needs to make its own codes.
    • No: calls POST /v2/auth/credentials and saves only the JWT. In OTP states it takes a 6-digit code (or a seed, which it turns into a code). The JWT expires in 24 hours.
  4. Default license. Optionally pick one for the profile.

When a saved JWT has expired, connect() in a terminal starts again at step 3, so you're offered a secret key each time.

docs.title: How connect() finds a credential
docs.text:
import t3api_utils as t3

client = t3.connect()

connect() stops at the first of these that supplies a credential:

# Source Notes 1 connect(secret_key=...) or connect(jwt=...) Wins over everything. 2 T3_SECRET_KEY, then T3_JWT Best for CI and scheduled jobs. 3 The profile's saved secret key, or its JWT if it hasn't expired See which profile below. 4 The login flow Only when interactive allows it (below). - Otherwise Raises AuthRequired with setup instructions.

Then it validates the credential with one GET /v2/auth/whoami call. A rejected credential raises AuthError, and the client is closed for you. connect(validate=False) skips the check.

Prompts. By default connect() prompts only when someone can answer: a terminal, or a Jupyter notebook. It never prompts when stdin isn't a terminal, so a cron job or CI step without a credential fails at once instead of waiting for input. interactive=False never prompts; interactive=True allows it.

docs.title: Which profile
docs.text:
The profile is connect(profile=...), then T3_PROFILE, then the default profile in the config file.

The profile also supplies the API host and default license. When the credential comes from an argument or environment variable (steps 1 and 2), the default profile is not consulted for those, so T3_SECRET_KEY on its own always means the production host and no default license. Name a profile (profile= or T3_PROFILE) to use its settings alongside a key from the environment.

docs.title: Which API host
docs.text: connect(api_host=...), then T3_API_HOST, then the profile's api_host, then https://api.trackandtrace.tools.

docs.title: Which default license
docs.text:
connect(license=...), then T3_LICENSE, then the profile's license. It's available as client.license, and it's used only by calls whose endpoint requires a licenseNumber. A license passed to a call always wins.

In the sandbox, only connect(license=...) counts: T3_LICENSE and the profile's license are production licenses.

docs.title: Other connect() options
docs.text: Option Default What it does validate True Check the credential with /v2/auth/whoami. sandbox T3_SANDBOX, then False Swap the credential for a Metrc sandbox JWT. See Sandbox. spec T3_SPEC, then "auto" "bundled" pins the spec shipped with the package. See Endpoints and the spec. rate_limit 10.0 Requests per second across all threads. None turns it off. concurrency 10 Threads used to fetch collection pages. timeout 30.0 Request timeout in seconds. Reports always get 5 minutes. log_http T3_LOG_HTTP Log every request and response, secrets masked. verify, proxy True, None TLS verification and proxy URL, as in httpx2. transport None An httpx2 transport to use instead of the network (for tests).

docs.title: Profiles and where secrets live
docs.text:
A profile is a saved login. Non-secret settings go in config.toml in the user config folder:

OS Config folder macOS ~/Library/Application Support/t3api-utils/ Linux ~/.config/t3api-utils/ Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\t3api-utils\ config.toml
default_profile = "mo"

[profiles.mo]
api_host = "https://api.trackandtrace.tools"
metrc_hostname = "mo.metrc.com"
username = "jdoe"
license = "LIC-00001"        # optional default
credential = "secret_key"    # or "jwt"

Secrets are not in that file. They go in the OS keyring under the service name t3api-utils, with the entry <profile>:secret_key or <profile>:jwt: macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or Secret Service on Linux.

No keyring? On headless Linux or in a container there may be no keyring backend. If a keyring write fails, the secret goes in secrets.toml next to config.toml, created readable only by you, and a warning says so. For CI, skip profiles and use T3_SECRET_KEY.

Manage profiles from the command line:

t3api login --profile mi-prod      # create or update a profile
t3api profiles list                # show them all; the default is ticked
t3api profiles use mi-prod         # make it the default
t3api profiles remove mi-prod      # delete it and its saved secret
t3api license set LIC-00001 -p mi-prod
t3api logout -p mi-prod            # forget the saved credential, keep the profile

The first profile you create becomes the default.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
These are the only environment variables the library reads. There's no .t3.env file.

Variable What it does T3_SECRET_KEY Secret key to use. Wins over any saved profile. T3_JWT JWT to use, if T3_SECRET_KEY isn't set. T3_PROFILE Profile to use instead of the default. t3api commands that take --profile read it too. T3_LICENSE Default license number. Ignored in the sandbox. T3_SANDBOX 1, true, yes or on makes connect() and the t3api data commands use the Metrc sandbox. T3_API_HOST T3 API base URL, e.g. a staging host. T3_SPEC bundled pins the spec shipped with the package. T3_LOG_HTTP 1, true, yes or on logs every request and response at DEBUG. T3_LOG_FILE With T3_LOG_HTTP, write that log to this file.

docs.title: Scheduled jobs and CI
docs.text:
Set T3_SECRET_KEY from your CI system's secret store and call connect() with no arguments:

.github/workflows/nightly.yml (excerpt)
env:
  T3_SECRET_KEY: ${{ secrets.T3_SECRET_KEY }}
  T3_LICENSE: LIC-00001
steps:
  - run: uv run nightly_export.py
nightly_export.py
import t3api_utils as t3

with t3.connect(interactive=False) as client:
    rows = client.collect("METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES")
    t3.to_csv(rows, "packages.csv")

interactive=False is the default behaviour without a terminal anyway; passing it makes the intent clear. If the key is missing, the job fails with AuthRequired and instructions instead of waiting for input.

docs.title: Managing secret keys
docs.text:
A secret key's ID is the key value itself, so rotate and delete take the key.

Python (client.secret_keys) CLI Endpoint list() t3api keys list (keys masked) GET /v2/auth/secretkey create(hostname, username, password, email=None, otp_seed=None) t3api keys create POST /v2/auth/secretkey rotate(key, password=..., username=None, hostname=None, email=None, otp_seed=None) t3api keys rotate [KEY] PUT /v2/auth/secretkey/{key} delete(key) t3api keys revoke KEY DELETE /v2/auth/secretkey/{key} 
for key in client.secret_keys.list():
    print(key["isEnabled"], key["isManaged"], key["lastUsedAt"])

After a Metrc password, email or OTP change, the key stops working: requests fail with AuthError and a hint to rotate. Rotating updates the Metrc login stored behind the key. The key value stays the same, so nothing that uses it needs changing:

t3api keys rotate

With no argument it rotates the profile's saved key. In Python, client.secret_keys.rotate(key, password="...") fills in the username and hostname from the profile, or from whoami.

To cut a key off, delete it. Anything using it stops working, including report URLs that contain it. Managed keys can't be deleted (the server answers 403).

t3api keys revoke 1b2c3d4e-...

Logging out. t3api logout removes the profile's saved secret from this machine; the key itself still works. t3api logout --everywhere also calls POST /v2/auth/logout, which ends all of the account's Metrc sessions.

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text:
connect(sandbox=True) exchanges your credential for a Metrc sandbox JWT through POST /v2/auth/sandbox. Everything the client does after that, including submit=True writes, goes to the Metrc sandbox instead of production:

with t3.connect(sandbox=True) as client:
    lic = client.pick_license()        # the sandbox's own licenses
    client.post("/v2/items/discontinue", license=lic, json={"id": 12345}, submit=True)

To point an existing script or scheduled job at the sandbox without editing it, set T3_SANDBOX=1. The t3api command takes --sandbox before the command name (t3api --sandbox pull ...); see the CLI guide.

Licenses. The sandbox has its own licenses (such as SF-SBX-1-101), and it answers a request for any other license with an empty result, not an error. A production license would quietly return nothing. So in the sandbox:

  • T3_LICENSE and the profile's default license are ignored, and client.license is None unless you passed connect(license=...). The common license or client.license or client.pick_license() pattern then asks you to pick a sandbox license.
  • The first time a call names a license, the client lists the session's licenses (one request, cached) and logs a warning for any license that isn't one of them.

Telling where you are. client.sandbox is True in the sandbox, and client.hostname is the Metrc hostname behind the credential, such as sandbox-me.metrc.com (from whoami). Entering the sandbox logs Using the Metrc sandbox (sandbox-me.metrc.com). at INFO, and bulk(submit="ask") says "sandbox" when it asks.

The client's credential is a JWT from then on (client.credential_kind == "jwt"), so report_url(), which needs a secret key, isn't available. An existing client can switch with client.enter_sandbox(), which also clears client.license.

docs.title: Using a credential directly
docs.text:
connect() is the usual way in, but T3Client can be built by hand with one of the two httpx2.Auth classes:

client = t3.T3Client(auth=t3.SecretKeyAuth("..."), license="LIC-00001")

This skips profiles, environment variables and validation entirely.

docs.title: The t3api command
docs.text:
Installing t3api-utils adds a t3api command. It covers logging in, profiles, secret keys, and the common data tasks, without writing Python.

t3api --help
t3api pull --help

How to run it:

Setup Command Installed with pip, or uv tool install t3api-utils t3api ... In a uv project that depends on t3api-utils uv run t3api ... Nothing installed uvx --from t3api-utils t3api ...

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Profiles. Every command that uses a credential takes --profile / -p. Without it, the profile is T3_PROFILE, then the default profile, then one named default. Credentials are found the same way as connect(), so T3_SECRET_KEY works here too.
  • Licenses. --license / -l takes a license number. On pull and report, repeat it for several licenses. Leave it out to use the profile's default license.
  • Output. Data (tables, IDs, URLs) goes to stdout. Messages, prompts and progress go to stderr, so t3api ... > file captures only the data.
  • Exit codes. 0 on success, 1 on an error (with a red ✗ message), 130 when cancelled with Ctrl-C.
  • Global options, before the command: --verbose / -v shows the library's progress logs, --version prints the version, and --sandbox uses the Metrc sandbox.
  • Sandbox. t3api --sandbox COMMAND (or T3_SANDBOX=1) runs whoami, pull, report and the tag-lists commands against the Metrc sandbox. The profile's default license is ignored there, so pass -l with a sandbox license (or pick one when asked). login, logout, keys and license manage the credential and the profile, and always use the real account.
t3api --sandbox whoami
t3api --sandbox pull METRC_ACTIVE_PLANTBATCHES -l SF-SBX-1-101 -o batches.csv

docs.title: login
docs.text:
t3api login [--profile P] [--host URL]

Runs the login flow: paste an existing secret key, or log in with Metrc credentials and accept the offer to create one. Saves it to the profile (creating the profile if needed) and optionally sets a default license. The first profile becomes the default.

--host sets the T3 API base URL for the profile. It defaults to T3_API_HOST, then the profile's saved host, then https://api.trackandtrace.tools.

docs.title: logout
docs.text:
t3api logout [--profile P] [--everywhere]

Removes the profile's saved credential from the keyring (or secrets file). The profile and its settings stay. A secret key itself keeps working; delete it with t3api keys revoke if it's no longer needed.

--everywhere first calls POST /v2/auth/logout, which logs out all of the account's Metrc sessions.

docs.title: whoami
docs.text:
t3api whoami [--profile P]

Shows the profile, credential type, API host and default license, plus the username, Metrc hostname and subscription details T3 reports. With t3api --sandbox whoami it adds a sandbox row and shows the sandbox's hostname.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
t3api profiles list              # every profile; the default is ticked
t3api profiles use NAME          # make NAME the default
t3api profiles remove NAME       # delete NAME and its saved credential

profiles list shows each profile's credential type, Metrc host, username, default license and API host. Secrets are never shown.

docs.title: Default license
docs.text:
t3api license [--profile P]                # show it
t3api license pick [--profile P]           # choose from the account's licenses
t3api license set LIC-00001 [--profile P]  # set it directly

Scripts pick it up as client.license, and calls that need a license use it when you leave license= out.

docs.title: Secret keys
docs.text:
t3api keys list [--profile P]
t3api keys create [--profile P]
t3api keys rotate [KEY] [--profile P]
t3api keys revoke KEY [--profile P] [--yes]
Command What it does keys list Every secret key on the account, masked to the last 4 characters, with whether it's enabled, managed, when it was created and last used, and which one this profile uses. keys create Asks for Metrc hostname, username and password (plus email or OTP seed where the state needs them), creates a key, prints it once, and offers to save it to the profile. keys rotate After a Metrc password, email or OTP change: asks for the new login details and updates the key. The key value doesn't change. Without KEY, rotates the profile's saved key. keys revoke Deletes a key after asking for confirmation (--yes skips the question). Anything using it stops working, including report URLs that contain it. Removes it from any profile that saved it.

See Managing secret keys.

docs.title: endpoints
docs.text:
t3api endpoints [QUERY] [--kind KIND] [--profile P]

Searches the T3 spec. Every word of QUERY must appear in the endpoint ID, path, summary or tags. --kind / -k is one of collection, report, metrc_write, immediate_write, file, object or other.

t3api endpoints harvest
t3api endpoints transfers incoming --kind collection
t3api endpoints --kind report

It needs no credential, only the spec. T3_SPEC=bundled t3api endpoints ... works offline.

docs.title: pull
docs.text:
t3api pull [ENDPOINT] [-l LIC]... [-f FILTER]... [--sort S] [--mask FIELDS] [-o FILE] [--inspect] [-p P]

Loads a whole collection, as client.collect() does, and writes it to a file or opens it in the inspector.

Option What it does ENDPOINT A collection's endpoint ID or path. Leave it out to pick one from a searchable table. -l, --license License number. Repeat for several. Without it, the profile's default license is used, or you're asked to pick one. -f, --filter field__op:value. Repeat for several (all must match). --sort field:asc or field:desc. --mask Comma-separated fields to return. -o, --output File to write. .json writes JSON, .jsonl JSON Lines, anything else CSV. Without it, a CSV named after the data model, license and time. --inspect Open the rows in the inspector instead of writing a file (needs [tui]). 
t3api pull METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES -l LIC-00001 -o packages.csv
t3api pull METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS -l LIC-00001 -l LIC-00002 -f name__contains:flower --sort name:asc -o items.json
t3api pull /v2/harvests/active --mask id,name,currentWeight
t3api pull --inspect

docs.title: report
docs.text:
t3api report ENDPOINT [-l LIC]... [--format F] [-o FILE] [--columns C] [-f FILTER]... [--sort S] [--url] [-p P]

Downloads a server-side report.

Option What it does ENDPOINT A report's endpoint ID or path, e.g. ITEMS_REPORT. -l, --license License number. Repeat for up to 20. --format csv, xlsx, json or googleSheets. Defaults to the extension of -o, else csv. -o, --output File to write. Without it, <ENDPOINT>__<time>.<format> in the current folder. --columns Comma-separated columns. -f, --filter, --sort As for pull. --url Print a report URL containing the secret key instead of downloading. See the warning.

With --format googleSheets, it prints the new sheet's URL.

t3api report ITEMS_REPORT -l LIC-00001 -o items.xlsx
t3api report ACTIVE_PACKAGES_REPORT -l LIC-00001 -l LIC-00002 --columns label,quantity,locationName -o packages.csv
t3api report ACTIVE_PACKAGES_REPORT -l LIC-00001 --url

docs.title: inspect
docs.text:
t3api inspect FILE

Opens a JSON, JSON Lines or CSV file in the inspector. Needs the [tui] extra.

docs.title: Tag lists
docs.text:
t3api tag-lists list [-l LIC] [-p P]
t3api tag-lists create FILE --column COL [--name N] [--endpoint E] [-l LIC] [--shared] [-p P]
t3api tag-lists resolve LIST_ID [--endpoint E] [-o FILE] [-p P]
Command What it does tag-lists list Your tag lists with their ID, name, license, endpoint, entry count and scanned count. tag-lists create Creates a list from one column (--column / -c) of a CSV or TSV file. --name defaults to the file name. --endpoint / -e sets the collection it resolves against by default. --shared makes it visible to everyone with access to the license. Prints the new list's ID on stdout. tag-lists resolve Resolves a list to its objects and writes them like pull does (-o picks CSV, JSON or JSON Lines). --endpoint / -e resolves against a different collection. If any handle doesn't resolve, prints a table of them and exits 1. 
LIST_ID=$(t3api tag-lists create labels.csv -c label -e METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES --name "Room A")
t3api tag-lists resolve "$LIST_ID" -o room-a.csv

See Tag lists.

docs.title: The spec
docs.text:
t3api spec info [-p P]
t3api spec refresh [-p P]

spec info shows which copy of the T3 OpenAPI spec is in use (cached, live, stale or bundled), how old it is, its version, and how many operations of each kind it has. spec refresh fetches the live spec now and caches it, for example right after T3 announces a new endpoint. See Where the spec comes from.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
A collection is any paginated list endpoint: active packages, items, harvests, transfers, plants and so on. collect() loads all of it.

import t3api_utils as t3

with t3.connect() as client:
    packages = client.collect("METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES", license="LIC-00001")

The result is a list[dict], each row exactly as the API returns it. Nothing is renamed or dropped, and fields T3 adds later show up without a library change. Every row carries its licenseNumber.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
client.collect(
    "METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS",
    license="LIC-00001",
    filter=["name__contains:flower", "productCategoryName__contains:bud"],
    filter_logic="and",
    sort="name:asc",
    mask=["id", "name", "productCategoryName"],
    page_size=500,
)
Argument What it does license One license number, or a list (see several licenses). Defaults to the client's default license. filter One field__operator:value string, or a list of them. filter_logic "and" (the server's default: every filter must match) or "or" (any). sort field:asc or field:desc. One field, root level only. mask Fields to return, as a list or comma-separated string. Dotted paths such as item.name work. Smaller rows load faster. page_size Rows per request. Default 100; the server allows up to 500 on most collections, which means fewer requests. progress Show a progress bar. On by default when stderr is a terminal. params Any other query parameters, by their spec names.

Path parameters, for the few collections that have them, are keyword arguments.

docs.title: Filter operators
docs.text:
Filters run on the server, before paging, and string comparisons ignore case.

Field type Operators String contains, doesnotcontain, eq, neq, startswith, endswith Number, date-time lt, lte, eq, neq, gt, gte Boolean eq (true or false)

Date-times are ISO 8601, for example packagedDate__gte:2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z. A filter on a field the collection doesn't have fails with a 400 that lists the fields it accepts. Packages also accept four nested item fields: item.name, item.strainName, item.productCategoryName and item.unitThcContent.

on_hold = client.collect(
    "METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES",
    license="LIC-00001",
    filter=["isOnHold__eq:true"],
)
large_or_old = client.collect(
    "METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES",
    license="LIC-00001",
    filter=["quantity__gte:1000", "packagedDate__lt:2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"],
    filter_logic="or",
)

docs.title: How loading works
docs.text:
1. The endpoint is resolved to its collection operation. Anything else raises SpecError.
  2. Page 1 is fetched. Its totalPages says how many more there are.
  3. The remaining pages are fetched in parallel on a thread pool (10 workers by default), all through one rate limiter (10 requests per second by default).
  4. Rows come back in page order.

Change the defaults on connect():

client = t3.connect(rate_limit=5, concurrency=4)

Failures. A page that still fails after retries fails the whole call, and the error notes which page it was. collect() never returns partial results silently.

Data that changes while loading. Pages are read at slightly different moments. If rows are added or removed mid-load, a row can shift from one page to the next and be read twice. collect() drops any row whose id it has already seen and logs how many it dropped. A row that shifts the other way, into a page that was already read, can't be recovered. If you need an exact snapshot, load at a quiet time or use a report.

docs.title: Several licenses
docs.text:
Pass a list to load each license in turn and join the results:

licenses = [lic["licenseNumber"] for lic in client.licenses()]
packages = client.collect("METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES", license=licenses)

Each row's licenseNumber tells you where it came from.

docs.title: Large collections
docs.text:
iter_rows() takes the same arguments as collect() (except progress) but yields rows as each page arrives, one page at a time, so memory stays flat:

import csv

with t3.connect() as client, open("packages.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    for row in client.iter_rows("METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES", license="LIC-00001", mask=["label", "quantity"]):
        writer.writerow([row["label"], row["quantity"]])

It fetches pages one after another rather than in parallel, so it's slower than collect() for collections that fit in memory.

docs.title: One object
docs.text:
Collections with an {object_id} route share their endpoint ID with it:

item = client.get("METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS", object_id=12345, license="LIC-00001")
package = client.get("METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES", object_id=67890, license="LIC-00001")

object_id is the record's Metrc id.

docs.title: Super collections and include=
docs.text:
Super collections (/v2/packages/active/super, /v2/items/super, /v2/processingjobs/active/super and others, with IDs like METRC_ACTIVE_SUPERPACKAGES) attach related data to each row. Pick what to attach with include=, a list:

packages = client.collect(
    "METRC_ACTIVE_SUPERPACKAGES",
    license="LIC-00001",
    include=["labResults", "sourceHarvests"],
)
item = client.get("METRC_ACTIVE_SUPERITEMS", object_id=12345, license="LIC-00001", include=["history"])

collect(), iter_rows() and get() take it. Each value is sent as its own include parameter, which is what the server needs: a comma-joined include=labResults,sourceHarvests gets a 400. A comma-separated string is split for you.

Each collection allows its own values. For packages they're labResults, labResultBatches, sourceHarvests, history and coaResults; for items, notes, history, ingredients and images. To see them for any endpoint:

client.spec.endpoint("METRC_ACTIVE_SUPERPACKAGES", kind="collection").param("include").choices

A value the spec doesn't list logs a warning and is sent anyway, in case your copy of the spec is behind the server.

docs.title: Licenses and the default license
docs.text:
license= can be left out when the client has a default license (connect(license=...), T3_LICENSE, or the profile's). It's filled in only for endpoints that require a licenseNumber. A license passed in the call always wins.

client = t3.connect(license="LIC-00001")
items = client.collect("METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS")   # uses LIC-00001

docs.title: Picking interactively
docs.text:
For scripts a person runs in a terminal:

with t3.connect() as client:
    lic = client.license or client.pick_license()
    endpoint = client.pick_endpoint()            # collections, searchable
    rows = client.collect(endpoint.id or endpoint.path, license=lic)

Both pickers raise NotInteractive without a terminal, and Ctrl-C raises KeyboardInterrupt to your script. pick_license() returns at once, without asking, when the account has only one license.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
t3api pull METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES -l LIC-00001 -o packages.csv
t3api pull METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS -l LIC-00001 -l LIC-00002 --filter name__contains:flower -o items.json
t3api pull --inspect          # pick a collection, then browse it

See The t3api command.

docs.title: Endpoints and the spec
docs.text: The library has no hand-written method per endpoint. Everything it knows about endpoints, such as their paths, parameters and whether they're paginated, comes from the T3 OpenAPI spec, read at runtime. When T3 adds an endpoint, it works in your script as soon as the library sees the new spec, without an upgrade.

docs.title: Naming an endpoint
docs.text:
Every method that calls the API takes an endpoint as its first argument, in one of two forms:

An endpoint ID, the spec's x-t3-endpoint-id:

client.collect("METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES", license="LIC-00001")

A path from the spec, either as a template or filled in:

client.collect("/v2/packages/active", license="LIC-00001")
client.get("/v2/items/{object_id}", object_id=12345, license="LIC-00001")
client.get("/v2/items/12345", license="LIC-00001")

Path parameters such as {object_id} or {tag_list_id} are keyword arguments. Query parameters the library doesn't name itself go in params=.

One ID can name several operations. METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS is both GET /v2/items (the collection) and GET /v2/items/{object_id} (one item). The method you call picks between them: collect() takes the collection, get(..., object_id=...) takes the single-object route, and report() takes a report.

Writes use paths. In today's spec, routes that write to Metrc don't have endpoint IDs, so name them by path: client.post("/v2/items/discontinue", ...).

docs.title: Finding endpoints
docs.text:
From the command line:

t3api endpoints                          # everything
t3api endpoints harvest                  # every word must appear in the ID, path, summary or tags
t3api endpoints package --kind report    # narrow by kind

From Python, through client.spec:

client.spec.find("harvest", kind="collection")   # list[Endpoint]
client.spec.list(kind="report")                  # every report
client.spec.endpoint("METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS", kind="collection")
client.spec.ids()                                # every endpoint ID, sorted

Each Endpoint has:

Attribute Example id "METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS", or None for routes without one method "GET" path "/v2/items" kind "collection" (see below) tags ("Items",) summary "List of active items" params the operation's parameters, each with name, location, required, description and schema body_type "array" or "object" for routes with a JSON body, else None. body_is_array is True for the list routes.

ep.param("licenseNumber") returns one parameter, and ep.label() gives a readable GET /v2/items (METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS). A parameter's choices are the values the spec allows, such as a super collection's include values, or () when it doesn't list any.

In a terminal, client.pick_endpoint() shows a numbered table of collections that you can narrow by typing. client.pick_endpoint(kind=None) shows every endpoint, and kind="report" shows reports.

Some collections have a companion fields route that lists the fields you can filter on, for example:

client.get("/v2/items/fields", license="LIC-00001")

docs.title: Endpoint kinds
docs.text:
Each operation in the spec gets exactly one kind, worked out from its structure. The rules are checked top to bottom:

Kind Rule Count today Call it with collection GET whose 200 response is paginated (uses the spec's Pagination schema) 187 collect(), iter_rows() report Can respond with CSV or XLSX 83 report(), report_url() metrc_write Non-GET that takes the submit parameter 85 post() / put() / patch() / delete(), bulk() immediate_write Non-GET without submit 28 the same, without submit= file GET returning a PDF or an image 5 download() to a file, or get(), which returns bytes object GET with an {object_id} path parameter 144 get(..., object_id=...) other Everything else, e.g. /v2/licenses, /v2/auth/whoami 124 get() / request()

The counts come from the spec bundled with this release and will drift. The rules don't depend on them. t3api spec info shows the counts for the copy you're using.

Calling a method on the wrong kind raises SpecError and lists what the ID does have, for example collect() on a report.

docs.title: Parameter checks
docs.text:
Before sending anything, the client resolves the operation's parameters from the spec:

  • A missing required parameter raises SpecError before any request goes out, naming it the way you'd pass it: GET /v2/items (METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS) needs: license=.
  • A missing required body raises SpecError: needs a request body (json=...).
  • An unknown query parameter logs a warning and is sent anyway. Your cached spec can lag the server, and a hard error would block a parameter T3 has only just added.

The common collection parameters have Python names:

Python Query parameter license licenseNumber filter (string or list) one filter= per item filter_logic filterLogic sort sort mask (string or list) collectionMask, comma-joined include (string or list) one include= per item page_size pageSize

page, submit and secretKey are managed by the library; don't pass them in params=.

docs.title: Calling any endpoint
docs.text:
client.request() is the general form behind get(), post() and the rest:

client.request("GET", "/v2/tag-lists/{tag_list_id}/entries", tag_list_id="abc123")
client.request("GET", "/v2/saved-reports", params={"pageSize": 50})

It returns parsed JSON for JSON responses, bytes for anything else (PDFs, images, CSV), and None for an empty body. Non-2xx responses raise an APIError subclass.

get() on a collection returns only the first page, as the raw response. Use collect() for all of it.

docs.title: Where the spec comes from
docs.text:
The spec is loaded the first time something needs it, never at import, and at most once per client. Raw client.http calls never need it.

  1. Cached copy. A live copy is cached per API host, so a sandbox or staging host gets its own. A copy less than an hour old is used as is. An older one is revalidated with If-None-Match; an unchanged spec costs one small 304 response.
  2. Live fetch from <api host>/v2/spec/openapi.json (5 second timeout), saved to the cache.
  3. Stale cache, if the fetch fails. A warning says so.
  4. Bundled copy, the gzipped spec that ships inside the package.

The cache lives in the user cache folder: ~/Library/Caches/t3api-utils/spec/ on macOS, ~/.cache/t3api-utils/spec/ on Linux, and %LOCALAPPDATA%\t3api-utils\Cache\spec\ on Windows.

Other controls:

  • connect(spec="bundled") or T3_SPEC=bundled pins the bundled copy. Use it for reproducible runs, or offline.
  • t3api spec info shows which copy is in use, how old it is and the count of each kind. t3api spec refresh forces a fresh fetch.
  • client.refresh_spec() does the same from Python.
  • client.spec.source.describe() says which copy a client loaded.

An endpoint that isn't in the spec raises UnknownEndpoint, with close matches when there are any:

'METRC_ACTIVE_ITEM' is not in the T3 OpenAPI spec. Close matches: METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS, ...

If T3 added the endpoint recently, t3api spec refresh picks it up.

docs.title: The escape hatch: client.http
docs.text:
client.http is the underlying httpx2.Client, already configured with your credential, the base URL, retries, rate limiting and HTTP logging. Use it for routes that aren't in the published spec, or when you want the raw response:

response = client.http.get("/v2/anything-new", params={"licenseNumber": "LIC-00001"})
response.raise_for_status()
data = response.json()

Calls through client.http skip the spec entirely: no endpoint lookup, no parameter checks, no default license, and non-2xx responses are returned rather than raised.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Every exception the library raises on purpose derives from t3.T3Error, and all of them can be imported from the top-level package.

T3Error
├── AuthRequired         no credential found, and no terminal to ask in
├── NotInteractive       a picker or prompt was called without a terminal
├── SpecError            missing required parameter, wrong endpoint kind
│   └── UnknownEndpoint  ID or path not in the spec
└── APIError             any non-2xx response
    ├── AuthError        401, 403
    ├── NotFound         404
    ├── ValidationError  400, 422
    │   └── TagListResolveError
    ├── RateLimited      429, after retries
    └── ServerError      5xx

SpecError and its subclass are raised before any request is sent, so fixing them never risks a duplicate write.

docs.title: What an APIError carries
Auth errors and their hints
docs.text: Situation Hint 401 with a secret key, server code METRC_LOGIN_FAILURE The Metrc login behind the key changed. Run t3api keys rotate (the key value stays the same). Other 401 with a secret key The key was deleted or disabled, or the Metrc login behind it changed. Run t3api keys rotate, or t3api login to save a new one. 401 with a JWT It expired (JWTs last 24 hours). Run t3api login. 403 The credential works but can't access this. Check the license number and the account's permissions.

docs.title: Other exceptions you may see
docs.text: Exception When ValueError Misuse that the library can spot locally: submit= on a route with no dry run, dynamic=True on a route without dynamic validation, more than 20 licenses on a report, an empty license list, a bad submit, on_error, batch_size or on_unmatched value, an unknown column in filter_rows(), an empty list given to t3.choose(). TypeError A path parameter the endpoint doesn't have. Query parameters go in params=. ImportError t3.inspect() without the [tui] extra. The message names the install command. NotInteractive A picker, prompt or bulk(submit="ask") with no terminal to ask in. See Prompts and pickers. KeyboardInterrupt Ctrl-C at a picker or prompt. The library never calls sys.exit(); it's up to your script. httpx2 transport errors The network failed for good after retries (DNS, connection refused, timeouts).

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
Retries are built into the client's transport, so they apply to every call, including those made through client.http.

Method Retried on Never retried GET, HEAD, OPTIONS Connection errors and timeouts; 429, 502, 503, 504 Other 4xx and 5xx POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE 429; connection failures before the request was sent 5xx, timeouts after sending, every other 4xx
  • At most 3 attempts, with exponential backoff and jitter: about 0.5 seconds before the second attempt and 1 second before the third. A Retry-After header from the server is honoured instead, up to 60 seconds.
  • Why writes are different. A 429 means T3 rejected the request outright, so sending it again is safe. A 5xx, or a timeout after the request went out, may mean the write already reached Metrc, so it's raised to you instead of being repeated. A write that gets a 400 is sent exactly once.
  • Each retry logs a warning on the t3api_utils logger.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
Each client has one rate limiter, shared by every request it makes, including the threads that fetch collection pages. The defaults are 10 requests per second and 10 paging threads. Change them on connect():

client = t3.connect(rate_limit=5, concurrency=4)    # gentler
client = t3.connect(rate_limit=None)                # no client-side limit

If T3 still answers 429 after the retries, the call raises RateLimited, with a hint to lower rate_limit or concurrency.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
Request Timeout Normal requests 30 seconds (connect(timeout=...) changes it) Report downloads 5 minutes Spec and /v2/states fetches 5 seconds (falls back to a cached or bundled copy)

Single calls take timeout= too: client.get(..., timeout=120).

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
The library logs to logging.getLogger("t3api_utils") and never configures handlers or the root logger itself. If your script doesn't set up logging, Python's fallback handler still prints warnings to stderr, but INFO messages such as dry-run notices stay hidden. To see everything:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
Level Examples WARNING Retries; a query parameter, or an include value, the spec doesn't list; a JSON body whose shape (list or object) doesn't match the route's; a license that isn't one of the sandbox session's; rows that failed validation in bulk(); a stale spec cache; no OS keyring; every report_url() call. INFO Dry-run notices (dry run: pass submit=True to send ... to Metrc); entering the sandbox (Using the Metrc sandbox (sandbox-me.metrc.com).) and the default license it ignores; duplicate rows dropped by collect(); the bulk() summary; falling back to the bundled spec.

The t3api command sets up its own Rich log output; -v shows INFO messages.

docs.title: HTTP logging
docs.text:
To see every request and response, turn on HTTP logging:

T3_LOG_HTTP=1 uv run my_script.py                         # to stderr
T3_LOG_HTTP=1 T3_LOG_FILE=t3_http.log uv run my_script.py  # to a file

or in code:

client = t3.connect(log_http=True)

Each request and response is logged at DEBUG on the t3api_utils.http logger, with method, URL, headers and body:

2026-11-23 14:05:09,112 t3api_utils.http → GET https://api.trackandtrace.tools/v2/items?pageSize=100&licenseNumber=LIC-00001 headers={..., 'x-t3-api-key': '***'} body=
2026-11-23 14:05:09,431 t3api_utils.http ← 200 GET https://api.trackandtrace.tools/v2/items?pageSize=100&licenseNumber=LIC-00001 headers={...} body={"data": [...], ...}

T3_LOG_FILE adds a file handler. Without it, a stderr handler is added only if nothing else would print the messages; if your script already configured logging, the messages go through your handlers.

What's masked. HTTP logs are meant to be safe to share with support:

  • The Authorization, X-T3-API-Key, Cookie and Set-Cookie headers.
  • The key in /v2/auth/secretkey/{key} paths and in any secretKey= query parameter.
  • These JSON body fields, at any depth: password, otp, otpSeed, secretKey, accessToken, refreshToken.
  • Form bodies aren't logged at all, and neither are non-JSON response bodies (CSV, XLSX, PDF). Logged bodies are cut off at 4,000 characters.

The rest of each body is logged as is, so HTTP logs still contain your Metrc data. Treat them like any other export.

docs.title: Local data
docs.text: Helpers for what happens after the data arrives: matching it against a file, writing it out, reading it back and looking through it. None of them make network calls.

docs.title: Filtering against a CSV
docs.text:
t3.filter_rows() keeps the rows that match a CSV or TSV file, or a list of dicts:

import t3api_utils as t3

with t3.connect() as client:
    packages = client.collect("METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES", license="LIC-00001")

wanted = t3.filter_rows(packages, "wanted.csv")
wanted.csv
label
1A4000000000000000000001
1A4000000000000000000002
Argument What it does rows The rows to filter, e.g. from collect(). match A CSV or TSV path, or a list of dicts. columns Columns to compare. Defaults to every column of the match file. on_unmatched What to do when a line of match finds no row: "warn" (log a warning, the default), "error" (raise ValueError) or "skip" (say nothing).

How matching works:

  • Every column must match. With a header of item.name,locationName, a row matches when both values are equal.
  • Dotted paths such as item.name reach into nested objects.
  • Values compare as trimmed strings, so 12345 in the CSV matches the number 12345 in a row, and true matches True.
  • Results follow the order of match, and each row appears at most once.
  • A column that no row has raises ValueError and lists the columns that do exist, which catches typos in the CSV header.

Match on some of the file's columns only:

t3.filter_rows(items, "input.csv", columns=["name"], on_unmatched="error")

or against a list built in code:

t3.filter_rows(items, [{"name": "Blue Dream Flower"}, {"name": "Gelato Pre-Roll"}])

Matching happens on your machine, after loading the whole collection. For a long list of tag labels, a server-side tag list avoids loading everything first.

filter_rows() never prompts. For an interactive script, ask for the file first with t3.pick_file() and pass the result in.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
t3.to_csv(rows, "packages.csv")
t3.to_json(rows, "packages.json")
t3.to_json(rows, "packages.jsonl", lines=True)

Both return the Path they wrote, and create missing folders.

to_csv(rows, path=None, *, columns=None, strip_empty=False)

  • Nested objects become dotted columns: item.name, item.productCategoryName.
  • Lists are written as JSON text, so they can be parsed back.
  • Empty values and None become empty cells.
  • Columns are ordered with the common identifying fields first (hostname, licenseNumber, retrievedAt, dataModel, index, id, label, name), then every other column alphabetically.
  • columns=[...] picks and orders the columns yourself, using the dotted names.
  • strip_empty=True drops columns that are empty in every row.
  • The file is UTF-8 with a byte-order mark, so Excel on Windows opens it without garbling accents and symbols.

to_json(rows, path=None, *, lines=False)

  • Indented JSON, exactly as the API returned it (no flattening).
  • lines=True writes JSON Lines: one object per line, which is easier to stream and append to.
  • It also accepts a single dict.

Default file names. Leave path out and the file goes in the current folder, named from the first row's data model and license plus the time, for example MetrcPackage__LIC-00001__2026-11-23T14-05-09.csv.

A folder as the path. Pass a folder that exists, or a path ending in /, and the file gets the default name inside it. The folder is created if needed:

t3.to_csv(rows, "output/")      # output/MetrcPackage__LIC-00001__2026-11-23T14-05-09.csv
t3.to_json(rows, "output/", lines=True)

docs.title: Reading files back
docs.text:
t3.read_rows() reads JSON, JSON Lines, CSV or TSV into a list of dicts:

rows = t3.read_rows("packages.json")

A JSON file holding a T3 response envelope ({"data": [...], ...}) gives you its data. Values read from CSV are strings.

docs.title: The inspector
docs.text:
t3.inspect() opens a full-screen terminal viewer that shows one row at a time as formatted JSON:

t3.inspect(rows, title="Active packages")
Key Action Left / Right Previous / next row Home / End First / last row / Search every nested value Ctrl+L Clear the search ? Help Q or Esc Quit

It needs the tui extra, which installs Textual:

pip install "t3api-utils[tui]"
uv add "t3api-utils[tui]"

Without it, t3.inspect() raises an ImportError that names the install command. Textual is imported only when you call inspect(), so scripts that don't use it pay nothing.

From the command line, t3api inspect FILE opens a JSON, JSON Lines or CSV file, and t3api pull ENDPOINT --inspect opens a collection straight from the API.

docs.title: Picking a file
docs.text:
t3.pick_file() lists the CSV, TSV, JSON and JSON Lines files in a folder, newest first, as a numbered table, and returns the chosen Path:

path = t3.pick_file()                                # current folder
path = t3.pick_file("exports", patterns=["*.csv"])   # one folder, CSVs only

Type a number to choose, or some text to narrow the list. If the folder has no matching files, it asks for a path instead. Like every picker, it raises NotInteractive without a terminal, and Ctrl-C raises KeyboardInterrupt.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text:
This is scripts/example.py from the repository: pick a license and a collection, load all of it, browse it, then keep and save the rows that match input.csv.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = ["t3api-utils[tui]>=2.0"]
# ///
"""Pick a collection, load all of it, and browse the rows that match input.csv."""

from pathlib import Path

import t3api_utils as t3

INPUT = Path(__file__).with_name("input.csv")


def main() -> None:
    with t3.connect() as client:
        license = client.license or client.pick_license()
        endpoint = client.pick_endpoint(kind="collection")
        rows = client.collect(endpoint.id or endpoint.path, license=license)
        t3.inspect(rows, title=endpoint.id or endpoint.path)

        matches = t3.filter_rows(rows, INPUT, on_unmatched="warn")
        print(f"Saved {len(matches)} matching rows to {t3.to_csv(matches)}")
        t3.inspect(matches, title="matches")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Prompts and pickers
docs.text:
Scripts that a person runs in a terminal often need to ask something: which license, which package, how much, and "submit this?". The library's prompts cover that and match the look of its own pickers. Use them instead of input().

Function Asks for Returns t3.confirm(question, *, default=False) yes or no bool t3.ask(question, *, default=None, parse=None) a value str, or what parse returns t3.choose(title, items, columns, render, *, filterable=None) one item from a numbered table the item client.pick_license() one of the credential's licenses the license number client.pick_endpoint(kind="collection") an endpoint from the spec an Endpoint t3.pick_file(directory=".", *, patterns=...) a CSV, TSV, JSON or JSON Lines file a Path

docs.title: Without a terminal
docs.text:
All of them raise t3.NotInteractive when there's no terminal (or Jupyter kernel) to ask in, for example in a scheduled job or CI. They never wait for input that can't arrive. input() would raise EOFError or hang instead.

Ctrl-C raises KeyboardInterrupt to your script. The library never exits for you.

So every interactive script needs a way to run without asking. The usual pattern is a flag or an environment variable that supplies the answer:

license = args.license or client.license or client.pick_license()

docs.title: confirm()
docs.text:
if not t3.confirm(f"Create {len(items)} items in {license}?"):
    return

The default answer is no: pressing Enter declines. Pass default=True for questions where yes is the safe answer.

To confirm before a bulk write, bulk(submit="ask") already shows the validation results and asks. See Asking before submitting.

docs.title: ask()
docs.text:
from datetime import date

name = t3.ask("Item name")
quantity = t3.ask("Quantity", parse=float)
when = t3.ask("Date (YYYY-MM-DD)", default=date.today().isoformat(), parse=date.fromisoformat)

An empty answer takes default, or asks again when there isn't one. parse turns the text into something else. When it raises ValueError, the message is shown in red and the question is asked again, so parse=float and parse=date.fromisoformat need no extra checking. Any other exception from parse propagates.

docs.title: choose()
docs.text:
choose() shows a list of anything as a numbered table:

package = t3.choose(
    "Source package",
    packages,
    columns=["Label", "Item", "Quantity"],
    render=lambda p: [p["label"], p["item"]["name"], f'{p["quantity"]} {p["unitOfMeasureAbbreviation"]}'],
)

render(item) returns one string per column. The person types a number, or, when the list is filterable, some text to narrow it down. filterable defaults to on for more than 10 items. The table shows 40 rows at a time. An empty list raises ValueError.

pick_license(), pick_endpoint() and pick_file() are built on it. pick_license() returns at once, without asking, when the account has only one license.

docs.title: Reports and tag lists
docs.text: Both are built on the T3 server, so they do work that would otherwise take many requests and some local code.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
A report endpoint builds a whole collection into one CSV, XLSX or JSON file on the server. When you want a spreadsheet, it's usually quicker than collect() plus to_csv(). There are 83 report endpoints today:

t3api endpoints --kind report
t3api endpoints package --kind report

client.spec.list(kind="report")

docs.title: Downloading
docs.text:
import t3api_utils as t3

with t3.connect() as client:
    client.report("ITEMS_REPORT", licenses=["LIC-00001"], to="items.xlsx")

With to=, the report streams straight to the file (written to a temporary file first, then renamed, so a failed download never leaves half a file) and report() returns the path.

Argument What it does endpoint A report's endpoint ID (ITEMS_REPORT, ACTIVE_PACKAGES_REPORT, ...) or path. licenses One license or a list of up to 20. Defaults to the client's default license. More than 20 raises ValueError. format "csv", "xlsx", "json" or "googleSheets". Defaults to the extension of to (.csv, .xlsx, .json), else "csv". to File to write. columns Columns to include, in order, as a list or comma-separated string. Each report has its own default set. An unknown name fails with a 400 that lists the valid ones. filter, filter_logic, sort As in collect(). row_limit Return only the first this-many rows. delivery, email delivery="email" with email= asks the server to email the report instead. params Any other query parameters, by their spec names.

What comes back:

Call Returns to="..." The Path written no to, format="csv" or "xlsx" bytes no to, format="json" Parsed JSON: an envelope with data, filters, sort and so on format="googleSheets" The URL of a new Google Sheet. email= shares it with that address. delivery="email" The server's delivery receipt; the report arrives by email

Report downloads get a 5 minute timeout instead of the usual 30 seconds.

# Several licenses, chosen columns, filtered and sorted, to CSV
client.report(
    "ACTIVE_PACKAGES_REPORT",
    licenses=["LIC-00001", "LIC-00002"],
    to="packages.csv",
    columns=["label", "quantity", "unitOfMeasureAbbreviation", "locationName"],
    filter=["isOnHold__eq:false"],
    sort="label:asc",
)

# Straight into memory
csv_bytes = client.report("ITEMS_REPORT", licenses="LIC-00001", format="csv")

# Emailed instead of downloaded
client.report("ITEMS_REPORT", licenses="LIC-00001", format="xlsx",
              delivery="email", email="me@example.com")

Row caps. A report returns at most 50,000 rows, and a super report (.../super/report) at most 5,000. A collection larger than the cap is rejected rather than silently cut short. Narrow it with filter, or pass row_limit to ask for the first rows on purpose.

Saved reports and schedules (/v2/saved-reports) have no helper yet. Reach them with client.request():

client.request("GET", "/v2/saved-reports")

docs.title: Report URLs for spreadsheets
docs.text:
client.report_url() builds a report URL with your secret key in it, for Excel or Google Sheets to pull directly. It takes the same arguments as report(), except to, delivery and email, and format defaults to "csv":

url = client.report_url("ACTIVE_PACKAGES_REPORT", licenses=["LIC-00001"])

Paste the URL into Google Sheets as =IMPORTDATA("<url>"), or into Excel with Data → From Web. The spreadsheet refreshes from T3 whenever it reloads.

The URL is a credential

Anyone who has the URL can use your secret key, for anything the key can do. Every call logs a warning to remind you.

Rotating a key keeps the same key value, so it does not cut off a leaked URL. Deleting the key (t3api keys revoke KEY) is the only way. Consider a separate key just for spreadsheet URLs, so you can revoke it without breaking your scripts.

report_url() sends no request. It needs a secret key; with a JWT it raises T3Error, because a JWT in a URL would stop working within 24 hours.

From the command line: t3api report ACTIVE_PACKAGES_REPORT -l LIC-00001 --url.

docs.title: Tag lists
docs.text:
A tag list is a list of handles kept on the T3 server, usually Metrc tag labels. T3 resolves the list to the objects those handles stand for. It's the quickest way from a column of scanned labels to full package records, and the list can be shared with everyone on the license.

client.tag_lists wraps /v2/tag-lists.

docs.title: From a CSV to packages
docs.text:
labels.csv
label
1A4000000000000000000001
1A4000000000000000000002
1A4000000000000000000003

with t3.connect() as client:
    tl = client.tag_lists.from_csv(
        "labels.csv",
        column="label",
        license="LIC-00001",
        endpoint="METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES",
        name="Room A",
    )
    packages = tl.resolve()
    t3.to_csv(packages, "room-a-packages.csv")

endpoint is the collection the list resolves against by default. name defaults to the file name. A TSV file works the same way.

docs.title: Creating lists
docs.text:
Method Creates a list from create(name, license=None, endpoint=None, visibility="USER", handles=None, metadata=None) A list of handles (strings) or entry dicts from_csv(path, column, *, name=None, license=None, endpoint=None, visibility="USER") One column of a CSV or TSV file from_rows(rows, field, *, name, license=None, endpoint=None, visibility="USER") One field of each row, e.g. from collect(). Dotted paths such as item.name work.
  • license defaults to the client's default license.
  • visibility="USER" keeps the list to yourself. "LICENSE" lets anyone on the same Metrc hostname with access to the license read the list and add, remove and scan entries. Only the creator can rename or archive it.
  • Handles are trimmed, blanks are dropped, and repeats are skipped. Matching ignores case and surrounding whitespace, and so does the repeat check.
  • An entry can be a dict with more than a handle, such as {"handle": "1A4000000000000000000001", "name": "Vault shelf 3"}.
  • Each request carries at most 5,000 entries, so larger lists are sent in chunks. A list can grow past 5,000, but the server only resolves lists of up to 5,000 entries, so create() warns when a list is bigger. Split it to use resolve().

Each of these returns a TagList.

docs.title: Working with a list
docs.text:
A TagList has the list's fields and the client.tag_lists methods bound to its ID:

tl.id, tl.name, tl.license, tl.endpoint     # common fields
tl["entryCount"]                             # any field, from tl.data

tl.add(["1A4000000000000000000004"])         # {"created": 1, "updated": 0}
tl.remove(["1A4000000000000000000001"])      # counts, plus handlesNotFound
tl.scan(["1A4000000000000000000002"])        # mark as scanned
tl.entries()                                 # every entry
tl.update(name="Room A (done)")              # change fields, e.g. archived=True
tl.refresh()                                 # reload from the server

To find an existing list:

lists = client.tag_lists.list(license="LIC-00001")
tl = client.tag_lists.get(lists[0]["id"])

list() also takes visibility=, endpoint= and archived=.

docs.title: Resolving
docs.text:
resolve() returns the objects the list's handles stand for, in the order the entries were added, paged like a collection:

packages = tl.resolve()
superpackages = tl.resolve("METRC_ACTIVE_SUPERPACKAGES")
slim = tl.resolve(mask=["label", "item.name", "quantity"])

Each collection matches on one field, decided by the server: label for packages, plants and tags; packageLabel for transferred packages; manifestNumber for transfers; name for items, harvests, plant batches and strains. A list can be resolved against any of the collections T3 supports for tag lists, not just its default. include= attaches related data, and is only accepted with a /super collection.

All or nothing. If any handle matches no object, or more than one, the server rejects the whole resolve with a 422, and resolve() raises TagListResolveError. Its errors holds one dict per problem handle, with handle, reason (NOT_FOUND or AMBIGUOUS) and matchCount:

try:
    packages = tl.resolve()
except t3.TagListResolveError as exc:
    for problem in exc.errors:
        print(f"{problem['handle']}: {problem['reason']} ({problem['matchCount']} matches)")

Fix the CSV, tl.remove() the bad handles, or resolve against a different collection (for example inactive packages) and try again.

When tag lists don't fit, for example matching on a field the server doesn't match on, or on several columns at once, load the collection and use t3.filter_rows() instead.

COA extraction has no helper yet. Call the route directly: client.post("/v2/tag-lists/{tag_list_id}/coa-extraction", tag_list_id=tl.id, json={...}), with the body the T3 API docs describe.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
t3api tag-lists create labels.csv --column label --endpoint METRC_ACTIVE_PACKAGES --name "Room A"
t3api tag-lists list -l LIC-00001
t3api tag-lists resolve <list-id> -o room-a.csv

create prints the new list's ID on stdout, so a shell script can capture it. If resolve fails, it prints a table of the handles that didn't resolve.

docs.title: Two kinds of write
docs.text:
How a write behaves depends on the route's kind in the spec:

Route kind submit left out submit=True metrc_write (85 routes today: creating packages, discontinuing items, adjusting, finishing, ...) Dry run. T3 checks the request (see What a dry run checks) and nothing reaches Metrc. Sent to Metrc. immediate_write (28 routes: auth, tag lists, label layouts, saved reports, support tickets, photo uploads) Takes effect immediately. Raises ValueError: the route has no dry run.

So a forgotten submit=True costs you a harmless dry run, never an accidental change in Metrc. Passing submit= at all, True or False, to an immediate route raises ValueError, so you can't mistake one kind for the other.

Check a route's kind with t3api endpoints discontinue or client.spec.endpoint("/v2/items/discontinue").kind.

docs.title: What a dry run checks
docs.text:
A dry run is static validation: the request's format, required fields and types. It doesn't check whether the records a request names exist. A dry run that moves package id: 0 to location locationId: 0 passes.

So a dry run catches a missing field, a wrong type or a malformed body. It won't tell you that a package ID is wrong, or that Metrc will refuse the change. Check that the records exist yourself first, for example by loading them with collect() and matching on them. This is what bulk() means when it calls a row valid: it passed validation, not that Metrc will accept it.

dynamic=True on any write method or bulk() also asks T3 for the route's dynamic checks (applyDynamicValidation=true). What those cover varies by route, and some routes have none yet, so treat them as an extra and not as a guarantee. A route whose spec doesn't offer them raises ValueError.

docs.title: Array bodies
docs.text:
Most Metrc write routes (68 of 85 today) take a list of objects as the body, even when you send one. They include the common bulk jobs: adjusting, moving, finishing and noting packages; creating items and strains; and every plant, plant batch and harvest write. The others, such as /v2/items/discontinue, /v2/packages/discontinue and the void routes, take one object.

Send a list to a list route, even for one object:

client.post(
    "/v2/packages/change-locations",
    license=lic,
    json=[{"id": 123456, "locationId": 42, "actualDate": "2026-11-23"}],
)

The server answers a bare object on a list route with an unexplained HTTP 500, so the library logs a warning first when a json= body's shape doesn't match the spec. Check a route with client.spec.endpoint(path).body_is_array. bulk() handles this for you: you give it one dict per object, and it wraps them in a list for routes that take one.

docs.title: One write
docs.text:
import t3api_utils as t3

with t3.connect() as client:
    lic = "LIC-00001"

    # Dry run: validated by T3, not sent to Metrc
    result = client.post("/v2/items/discontinue", license=lic, json={"id": 12345})
    print(result.dry_run, result.message)      # True Dry run

    # The real thing
    result = client.post("/v2/items/discontinue", license=lic, json={"id": 12345}, submit=True)
    print(result.dry_run, result.message)      # False Success

post(), put(), patch() and delete() take:

Argument What it does endpoint A path (write routes don't have endpoint IDs in today's spec). license Fills licenseNumber. Defaults to the client's default license when the route requires one. json The request body. A list for array routes. params Other query parameters, by their spec names. files, data Multipart or form bodies, as in httpx2 (not on delete()). See Uploads. submit True sends a Metrc write for real. dynamic True also asks for the route's dynamic checks. See What a dry run checks. timeout Override the request timeout for this call. **path_params Path parameters such as tag_list_id=.

Each returns a WriteResult:

Attribute What it holds dry_run True if T3 only checked the request (statically) and nothing reached Metrc. message The server's message: "Dry run" or "Success" for Metrc writes. data The parsed response body. response The httpx2.Response.

Every dry run also logs dry run: pass submit=True to send ... to Metrc at INFO on the t3api_utils logger, so a script that forgot submit=True says so when logging is on.

Errors. A rejected write raises an APIError subclass, usually ValidationError (400 or 422), with the server's explanation in .detail and any per-field problems in .errors:

try:
    client.post("/v2/items/discontinue", license=lic, json={"id": 12345}, submit=True)
except t3.ValidationError as exc:
    print(exc.detail)

Never repeated. A write is retried only when T3 answered 429 (rate limited, so it was rejected) or the connection failed before the request was sent. A 5xx or a timeout after sending might mean the write reached Metrc, so it's raised to you instead of being sent again. See Retries.

docs.title: Uploads
docs.text:
Two routes take a file as multipart/form-data: POST /v2/items/images/file (an immediate write that uploads an item photo) and POST /v2/packages/labresults/document/file (a Metrc write, so a dry run unless submit=True). Pass the file with files=, in httpx's (name, content, content type) form, and any other form fields with data=:

from pathlib import Path

photo = Path("blue-dream.png")
client.post(
    "/v2/items/images/file",
    license=lic,
    files={"file": (photo.name, photo.read_bytes(), "image/png")},
)

Each route's entry in the T3 API docs names its form fields.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
Routes of kind file (manifest and COA PDFs, item photos) return bytes from get(). client.download() streams one straight to disk instead, through a temporary file that's renamed only when the download completes, so a failure never leaves half a PDF behind:

client.download(
    "/v2/transfers/manifest",
    f"manifests/{number}.pdf",
    license=lic,
    params={"manifestNumber": number},
)

It creates missing folders and returns the path.

docs.title: Many writes: bulk()
docs.text:
bulk() validates every row, then submits them. Give it one dict per object, whatever the route's body shape:

items = client.collect(
    "METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS",
    license=lic,
    filter=["name__startswith:TEST"],
    mask=["id", "name"],
)
result = client.bulk(
    "/v2/items/discontinue",
    rows=[{"id": item["id"]} for item in items],
    license=lic,
    submit=True,
    log_to="discontinue-results.csv",
)
print(result.summary())     # POST /v2/items/discontinue: 42 submitted

For a metrc_write route:

  1. Validate. Every row is sent as a dry run, and each result recorded. Remember that a dry run only checks format.

  2. Decide, according to submit:

    submit= What happens False (the default) Stops here and returns. Nothing is submitted. "ask" Shows the route, the license, the counts (and "sandbox" in the sandbox), lists any rows that failed, and asks whether to submit the rest. The default answer is no. True Submits without asking when every row passed. If some failed: in a terminal it shows them and asks whether to submit only the valid rows (default no); without a terminal it returns without submitting, unless on_error="skip", which submits the valid rows without asking.

  3. Submit: each valid row is sent with submit=true, in order. With on_error="stop" (the default), the first row that fails stops the rest; on_error="skip" carries on.

  4. Return a BulkResult. log_to= also writes it to a CSV file.

An AuthError stops bulk() immediately whatever on_error says, since every later row would fail the same way.

docs.title: Asking before submitting
docs.text:
submit="ask" is the validate, show, confirm, submit pattern in one call. Each row is validated once:

import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--yes", action="store_true", help="submit without asking")
args = parser.parse_args()

result = client.bulk(
    "/v2/packages/change-locations",
    rows=moves,
    license=lic,
    submit=True if args.yes else "ask",
)

── POST /v2/packages/change-locations ──
License: LIC-00001
Rows: 12 passed validation
ℹ A dry run checks format, required fields and types, not whether the records it names exist.
Submit 12 row(s) to Metrc for LIC-00001? [y/n] (n):

Without a terminal, submit="ask" raises NotInteractive before sending anything: "submit="ask" needs a terminal to ask in. Pass submit=True to submit without asking." A scheduled job that forgot --yes fails loudly instead of quietly submitting nothing.

confirm= is a different thing

confirm=True doesn't ask anything. It means "I know this immediate route has no dry run; send the rows anyway". To be asked, use submit="ask".

docs.title: Batches
docs.text:
Array routes take many objects in one request. batch_size=N sends up to N rows per request, in both the validation and submit passes:

client.bulk("/v2/packages/adjust", rows=adjustments, license=lic, submit=True, batch_size=50)

That's far fewer requests, but a request that fails marks every row in it with the same error, because the server answers for the whole request. The default, batch_size=1, keeps each row's error separate. batch_size above 1 on a route that takes one object raises ValueError.

docs.title: Validate first, submit later
docs.text:
Leave out submit=True to check every row without touching Metrc:

check = client.bulk("/v2/items/discontinue", rows=rows, license=lic)
if check.ok:
    client.bulk("/v2/items/discontinue", rows=rows, license=lic, submit=True)
else:
    for r in check.invalid:
        print(r.index, r.row, r.message)

The second call validates every row again before submitting. To show the results and decide in between without that, use submit="ask".

docs.title: Row statuses
docs.text: Status Meaning valid Passed validation (the dry run's static checks) and wasn't submitted (yet). It doesn't mean Metrc will accept it. invalid Failed validation. message says why. submitted Sent with submit=true and accepted. failed Sent with submit=true and rejected. message says why. not_sent Never sent, because an earlier row failed with on_error="stop".

docs.title: BulkResult
docs.text: Member What it gives you rows (or iterate the result) One RowResult per input row, in input order, with index, row, status, message, data and error (the APIError, if any). ok True when no row was invalid or failed. submitted True if the submit pass ran. invalid, failed The rows with that status. by_status("valid") The rows with any status. counts() {"submitted": 40, "failed": 2} and so on. summary() One line, e.g. POST /v2/items/discontinue: 40 submitted, 2 failed, or 12 passed validation, 1 failed validation before submitting. to_csv(path) One line per row: index, status, message, and the row as JSON.

docs.title: Immediate routes
docs.text:
Immediate routes have no dry run, so bulk() can't validate first. It refuses to run unless you pass confirm=True, or submit="ask" to have a person confirm in the terminal:

tl = client.tag_lists.create("Room A", license=lic)
labels = ["1A4000000000000000000001", "1A4000000000000000000002"]

client.bulk(
    "/v2/tag-lists/{tag_list_id}/entries",
    rows=[{"entries": [{"handle": label}]} for label in labels],
    method="POST",
    tag_list_id=tl.id,
    confirm=True,
)

(For tag lists, client.tag_lists is simpler; this only shows the shape.) method= picks the operation when a path has several write methods.

docs.title: A complete script
docs.text:
This is scripts/discontinue-items.py from the repository. It discontinues every item named in input.csv, which has a name column:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = ["t3api-utils>=2.0"]
# ///
"""Discontinue every item named in input.csv."""

from pathlib import Path

import t3api_utils as t3

INPUT = Path(__file__).with_name("input.csv")


def main() -> None:
    with t3.connect() as client:
        license = client.license or client.pick_license()
        items = client.collect("METRC_ACTIVE_ITEMS", license=license, mask=["id", "name"])
        matches = t3.filter_rows(items, INPUT, columns=["name"], on_unmatched="error")
        result = client.bulk(
            "/v2/items/discontinue",
            rows=[{"id": item["id"]} for item in matches],
            license=license,
            submit=True,
            log_to="discontinue-results.csv",
        )
        print(result.summary())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

on_unmatched="error" stops the script before any write if a name in the CSV doesn't match an active item.

bulk(client: T3Client, endpoint: str, rows: Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]], *, license: str | None = None, method: str | None = None, submit: bool | Literal['ask'] = False, confirm: bool = False, on_error: OnError = 'stop', log_to: str | Path | None = None, progress: bool | None = None, path_params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, dynamic: bool = False, batch_size: int = 1) -> BulkResult

Send many writes safely: validate every row, then submit.

For Metrc write routes:

  1. Every row is sent as a dry run and its result recorded. A dry run checks format, required fields and types, not whether the records a row names exist, so valid means "passed validation", not "Metrc will accept it".
  2. submit=False stops here. submit="ask" shows a summary (and any failures) and asks whether to submit, default no. submit=True carries on without asking unless some rows failed; then, in a terminal, it shows the failures and asks whether to submit only the valid rows. on_error="skip" submits them without asking.
  3. Each valid row is sent with submit=true, in order. With on_error="stop", the first failed submit stops the rest.

Each row is one object. On routes whose body is a list (most Metrc writes), rows are wrapped in a list for you.

Routes with no dry run (immediate_write) can't be validated first, so they need confirm=True ("I know this takes effect at once"), or submit="ask" to ask a person before sending.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default client T3Client

The client to send with.

required endpoint str

The write route's path (or endpoint ID).

required rows Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]]

One mapping per object to write.

required license str | None

Fills licenseNumber. Defaults to the client's license when the route requires one.

None method str | None

Picks the operation when a path has several write methods.

None submit bool | Literal['ask']

False validates only, True submits the valid rows, "ask" asks first. "ask" raises NotInteractive without a terminal, before sending anything, so a scheduled job can't hang or quietly submit nothing.

False confirm bool

Required for routes with no dry run, unless submit="ask".

False on_error OnError

"stop" (the default) or "skip", as described above.

'stop' log_to str | Path | None

Write the results to this CSV file.

None progress bool | None

Show progress bars. Defaults to on when stderr is a terminal.

None path_params Mapping[str, Any] | None

Values for the route's path parameters.

None dynamic bool

Also ask T3 for the route's dynamic checks (applyDynamicValidation). What they cover depends on the route.

False batch_size int

Rows per request, on routes whose body is a list. A request that fails marks every row in it with the same error, so the default of 1 keeps each row's error separate.

1

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

a bad submit, on_error or batch_size; an immediate route without confirm=True; batch_size above 1 on a route that takes one object; dynamic=True on a route without dynamic validation.

NotInteractive

submit="ask" without a terminal.

AuthError

the credential was rejected. It stops the run whatever on_error says.
